questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to try and study in an English-speaking country, and Boston seemed like a great university city due to the many universities located in the city. Also, I liked the fact that NYC is only a couple of hours away by train/bus and I had heard that New England should be very beautiful in the fall.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can highly recommend Boston and Boston University. I had a great semester there and enjoyed exploring the city as well as traveling and doing day trips on the weekends and during holidays. Boston is more European than many other cities in the US which made it easy to adapt, and it is historically a really interesting city. Boston University is a great university, and I especially appreciated all the facilities and benefits they offer to its students. The campus itself is located on a big road and is not the most charming one though. The good thing about it is the balance between being in the university campus bobble and still being in the middle of the city, which I think is one of the features that make Boston University special.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: You are very early on in the process assigned to a coordinator from Boston University who is reachable by e-mail and can answer all of your questions. This made the process upon arrival very manageable. Besides that, the university provides you with many resources on its website to help you figure everything out. You get the impression that they are very used to international/exchange students and have solutions for everything.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: When you arrive, there are three days of orientation before classes start, where you will get a lot of information and you will be able to ask all the questions you may have in terms of courses, visa, expenses, etc. You will also meet other students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: In terms of information and assistance, the orientation was very good. You get a lot of information, and they will cover everything you need to know and do. You will also meet the international coordinator whom you have been in contact with before arrival, and she will either be able to answer questions you have or put you in contact with a person who can. Regarding the social aspect, I was not completely satisfied with the orientation program. You are assigned to a group of freshmen/international students/exchange students with whom you spend the days, and I was lucky to be in a very good group where I met some really good friends, but there are not many social activities and therefore you need to reach out yourself and take initiative. Also, the orientation was both for freshmen and for exchange/international students meaning the other students you meet here are very young (freshmen are 17-18 years old), and a lot of the information you get and activities you do are not relevant for you. Overall, I was happy that there were these orientation days though because it was a good way to get familiar with the university and meet some other students before classes started.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are different options for on-campus housing. You can both choose a traditional dorm room (either private or with roommates), suite-style, or apartment-style where you have your own kitchen. All the on-campus housing options are very expensive though, and the only one I found affordable is the traditional dorm room with roommates. This was what I applied for, and I was assigned to a shared room with three roommates. Two of them were freshmen and were therefore very young, but the third was an exchange student like me and we became good friends.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: When you live on-campus a meal plan is mandatory because you don't have a kitchen. The meal plans are also quite expensive, but you can choose between different options. I chose the most common one, which is the 14 meals-per-week meal plan. This was perfect for me because I was often away on the weekends or wanted to eat out/elsewhere during the week, and therefore I didn't need more than these 14 meals per week plus the dining points, which are included and can be used on cafes/restaurants/bars/convenience stores on campus. The dining halls were better than I expected. They work like all-you-can-eat halls, where you check in with your BU-card, and then there are various food stands with different cuisines. Often the quality is not the best though, and there is a lot of American food, but for one semester it is okay.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: For me applying for on-campus housing was a last-minute decision. I had tried to look for rooms in shared apartments since spring but was only able to find 1-year leases, which wouldn't work for me since I was only there from September-December. Housing in Boston is in general very expensive (most of my friends paid 900-1400 dollars a month for a room off-campus) and it is very difficult to find any available rooms with a flexible lease. Also, there are a lot of scams so it can be difficult to find a place if you are not physically in Boston. I decided on on-campus housing because I wanted to be sure to have a place when I arrived in Boston, and I didn't want to spend more time looking for rooms before arriving. Also, I liked the idea of living in a central part of Boston, close to where I had classes in a social atmosphere with other students. The dorms are not the highest quality; you share a room and bathroom with others, but it is fine for one semester and reminded me a bit of efterskole or højskole.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I am very happy that I ended up on campus since most of my friends lived on campus too, and therefore we had lunch and dinner together every day in the dining halls which for me was a great way of socializing. I had the impression that exchange students living off-campus had to reach out more and had to be more active when it came to making friends. If you want to live off-campus I can recommend looking at Splitspot, June Homes, and Craigslist. Also, Boston University has its own housing page, where you can search for a room or a roommate.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you check your BU-mail regularly, which you set up after admission, and you register for courses as soon as registration opens, you'll be fine.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The course registration opens pretty early (in spring if you are doing a fall exchange). Course registration opens later for exchange students than for regular BU students, meaning some courses were already full when registration opened for us. I found this really annoying and also a bit unfair, but you can check regularly if somebody has dropped the course. You are able to add and drop courses during the first two weeks of the semester which I really enjoyed and took advantage of because you then are able to attend the first class to see whether you like the course and/or the professor or not (just remember to update your forhåndsgodkendelse from KU). It is also possible to write the professor if the class is full and ask if you can be enrolled anyway. I had success with this in one course, because I was very eager and wrote him before as well as showing up on the first day of class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always write Sage, the coordinator who is in charge of exchange students if you have any problems, or otherwise talk/write to professors.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to register for courses when registration opens. Check regularly to see if a spot opens if a course you want is full. Add all the courses you are considering, if you can, on your forhåndsgodkendelse from KU so you have the freedom to add and drop in the first two weeks of the semester if you realize that a course isn't what you expected. If a course you want is full, I can recommend the page
buninja.com
. Here you can list which course you want to get into, and then you'll get a sms/e-mail when a spot opens up (you'll need an American phone number to sign up though, so I only used it after arriving in Boston).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was overall happy about the levels of my courses because I didn't want to be too busy studying. I wanted to have time to travel, socialize and explore Boston, and therefore I tried not to pick too challenging courses. I had one 200-level course which was pretty easy, but I still found it very interesting because it was taught from an American perspective, which was new to me. I had two 500-courses, one of them was specifically for international students and was very easy too, while the criminology course was the only course, I felt matched my academic level. I didn't mind that the courses were maybe a bit too easy for me, because I still found much of the course material and discussions in class interesting since it was based on an American perspective and entailed discussions and topics that were new to me.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching differed a lot from what I am used to at KU. Your grade is not only based on one final exam as is the case on KU but on several assignments and participation. My classes were way smaller than at KU and it reminded me a lot of high school, where the professor knows the students' names, expects the students to participate and takes attendance (it affects your grade if you don't show up for class). In general, I found the workload during the semester higher than I am used to because you have quite a lot of quizzes, papers, presentations, etc. but the level of difficulty was lower, which made it manageable. Also, I really enjoyed that my grades didn't only depend on one final paper, which meant that the workload was spread out more evenly over the entire semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MET CJ 570 - Criminology and Crime Policy (4 credits)
MET MG 545 - American Institutions and Culture (4 credits)
CAS SO 242 - Globalization and World Poverty (4 credits)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the course Criminology and Crime Policy. I thought it was super interesting and professor Cadigan is very sweet and helpful.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to reschedule my flight home and in general, I didn't expect Boston to be as expensive as it is

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Phone plans can be quite expensive, but I can recommend phone carriers such as Mint Mobile and Red Pocket which are pretty cheap and more like Danish prices

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are more than 400 clubs at BU with all sorts of profiles. I joined the Unicef club, which was a great way of meeting American students and feeling more like a part of BU

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club, a sports team or volunteer

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
In Boston: take advantage of the free access for BU students at museums in Boston, enjoy the view of Boston from Washington Tower in Mount Auburn Cemetery, check out bars in Allston, go to BU ice hockey, basketball, and soccer games (even though you are not normally into sports)
Outside of Boston: Visit Cape Cod while the weather is still nice, visit Salem during Halloween, go to Providence during the WaterFire event, visit New Haven (Yale University is really beautiful), go to other states in New England for fall foliage (I can recommend New Hampshire and Maine), rent a car, do the Ocean Drive in Newport, Rhode Island, and enjoy the scenic view

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Boston is one of the most European cities in the States, and you can get around by foot or bike. Americans are generally very open compared to Danes and are more likely to approach strangers, which can be really nice when you are new and want to meet people.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Get to know your roommates or floormates (and try to accept the potential age difference), join a club or a sports team, talk to students from your classes

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Bars and clubs are very strict when it comes to ID, so always bring your passport when you are going out. The T is really slow and makes you appreciate the metro in Copenhagen. Always tip 15-20% even though it seems like a lot, and get used to always being asked "How are you?"

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The helpfulness and openness I experienced from Americans

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't panic if it takes a couple of weeks to adapt and unwind. I thought it was very exhausting at the beginning with all the small talk and new people and impressions, but you will find friends and have a great time.
2. Make sure to enjoy your time in Boston, go on trips, and do fun stuff. The semester is over before you know it, and then it's nice to have a lot of memories to look back at.
3. It is expensive to go on exchange, especially in Boston, and if you signed up to live on campus be aware that you will need to pay the full amount of rent + meal plan for your entire stay at the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember that KU transfers grades as pass/fail, so don't stress too much about them.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the amazing people I have met, trips and experiences I had, the improvement of my English skills, one of my classes in which I learned a lot

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Money matters, finding a place to live, being away from your people back home

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
